article_title: An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria
citation: Nwogo, E. U., Ihianle, I. K., Machado, P., Bird, J. J., Lotfi, A., Shuaib, A. A., Akinwumi, I. I., & Oluranti, J. (2026). An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15738
title: AI-enhanced personalised and adaptive learning platform: layered architecture integrating fine-tuned Pidgin-aware LLM, RAG, bilingual translation engine, and rule-based adaptive assessment
description: A modular, layered educational platform (presentation, application, AI services, data, and integration layers) delivering conversational AI, adaptive assessment, and multilingual content delivery. Its chatbot operates in Translate, Ask, and Ask/Translate modes, with web-based retrieval triggered "when the similarity score falls below a 60% threshold". RAG grounds LLM outputs in a vector database (Qdrant) to address static curricula and hallucination-prone generation, and the full implementation is publicly accessible as STEMHub.
requirements: Persistent learner data infrastructure (PostgreSQL and Qdrant) and backend APIs hosting the transformer-based language model and RAG components
constraints: Designed for resource-constrained deployment; quantisation trade-offs between semantic fidelity and inference latency constrain model choice
target_learners: Learners and educators in Nigerian multilingual, low-resource educational settings
target_learning_goals: Context-aware learning support, adaptive assessment, and personalised feedback in English and Nigerian Pidgin English
examples: Figures 13 and 14 show the integrated instructional environment with external resources and AI-generated assessments; the fine-tuned model is downloadable from Zenodo and Hugging Face
key_sources: Nwogo, E. U., Ihianle, I. K., Machado, P., Bird, J. J., Lotfi, A., Shuaib, A. A., Akinwumi, I. I., & Oluranti, J. (2026). An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15738

article_title: From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning
citation: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083
title: PIVOT: a three-stage pedagogy-guided instructional video tutoring framework
description: PIVOT is described as "a three-stage pedagogy-guided generative video tutoring framework for STEM education that supports active learning". Stage 1 generates structured instructional storyboards organizing objectives, prerequisite activation, explanations, visual plans, worked examples, and assessment probes. Stage 2 transforms the storyboard into shot-level Manim animations with a multimodal pedagogical verification harness covering layout, factual, and cognitive clarity, plus constrained layout prompting and automated code repair. Stage 3 generates storyboard-grounded quizzes and targeted remediation videos conditioned on learner responses, forming a closed feedback loop.
requirements: A learner-specified topic or learning goal as input
Storyboard generation must precede executable Manim code generation, narration synthesis, assessment construction, and multimodal verification
constraints: The system performs interaction-level adaptation conditioned on immediate learner responses rather than maintaining a fully personalized long-term learner model, with no long-term knowledge tracing or curriculum progression modeling
The multi-stage pipeline introduces substantially higher computational cost than direct multimedia synthesis approaches
target_learners: STEM learners at high-school and university level
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of STEM knowledge points in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and computer science
Correction of misconceptions through targeted remediation
examples: For the topic Bubble Sort, the storyboard specifies learning objectives, prerequisite activation of arrays and loops, a worked example on array [5, 1, 4, 2, 8], and an assessment probe on which element is fixed after the first pass
key_sources: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083

article_title: Archetypes or ability? Clustering for modelling student mathematical competence
citation: Benjamin Mawdsley, Tom Quilter, Richard Turner, Sarah Jackson, and Paul Edwards. (2026). Archetypes or ability? Clustering for modelling student mathematical competence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26063
title: Pinpoint Learning mock-exam dataset of 119,034 UK students across 13 national-level mock exams
description: A proprietary dataset from the Pinpoint Learning platform (https://www.pinpointlearning.co.uk/), which helps teachers track student performance by uploading mock exam results question by question. The authors state: "The data was extracted from the platform for thirteen different mock exams, involving a total of 119,034 unique students." Cleaning removed rows with negative scores (4 instances) and scores above full marks (7.5% of rows); each exam was sat by an average of 24137 students after cleaning.
requirements: Data is manually uploaded by teachers, so cleaning procedures are needed to remove contamination from scores entered for multiple questions at once
constraints: The data is proprietary and belongs to the platform, but is planned to be released at a future date
target_learners: UK GCSE mathematics students aged around 16
target_learning_goals: Predicting question-level mathematics performance and estimating student ability from mock exam results
examples: Students typically sat 2 or 3 of the 13 exams; scores ranged broadly with the bulk of grades around the 20% to 40% range

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Pintrich's SRL model: four phases crossed with four areas for regulation
description: Pintrich's model, presented in the first SRL handbook, structures SRL as four phases — forethought/planning/activation, monitoring, control, and reaction and reflection — each crossed with four areas for regulation: cognition, motivation/affect, behavior and context. The review notes this combination "offers a comprehensive picture that includes a significant number of SRL processes." The behavior-regulation area, covering "individual's attempts to control their own overt behavior," is unique among the six reviewed models, and the context area covers students' attempts to monitor, control and regulate the learning context.
requirements: The model is operationalized in research primarily through the MSLQ questionnaire built on Pintrich's empirical work
constraints: The review states there is no empirical evidence directly addressing validation of Pintrich's model itself, only MSLQ validation data
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning integrating motivation and cognition
examples: Schunk reviewed Pintrich's six major contribution areas, including the SRL-motivation relationship and classroom contexts

description: The study operationalizes ESL question development as "stage advancement in Pienemann and Johnston's developmental sequence for ESL question formation" (Pienemann & Johnston, 1987; Pienemann, Johnston, & Brindley, 1988). constraints: The measure captures development specifically for ESL question formation, not other L2 structures.
target_learning_goals: Development of English question formation
examples: Learners' stage assignment was tracked across four oral production tests over an 8-week period to detect stage advancement.

citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Pintrich's SRL model: four phases across cognition, motivation/affect, behavior, and context
description: Pintrich's model structures SRL as four phases, each with four areas for regulation. The review states that "SRL is compounded by four phases: (1) Forethought, planning and activation; (2) Monitoring; (3) Control; and (4) Reaction and reflection", each with regulation of cognition, motivation/affect, behavior, and context. The review highlights that Pintrich's is the only model analyzed that includes regulation of overt behavior, and that his questionnaire, the MSLQ, remains widely used in SRL research.

constraints: The review reports there is no empirical evidence directly addressing validation of Pintrich's model itself; empirical data exist on the MSLQ questionnaire
target_learning_goals: integration of motivation and strategy use in learning
examples: The MSLQ comprises 15 scales: a motivation section with 31 items and a learning strategies section with 50 items subdivided into cognitive, metacognitive, and resource management scales

citation: Pintrich, P.R. (2004). A Conceptual Framework for Assessing Motivation and Self-Regulated Learning in College Students. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 385–407. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-004-0006-x

description: The article presents a conceptual framework for assessing student motivation and self-regulated learning in the college classroom. It is explicitly grounded in a self-regulatory perspective: "The framework is based on a self-regulatory (SRL) perspective on student motivation and learning in contrast to a student approaches to learning (SAL) perspective." The framework is intended to guide assessment of motivation and learning among college students and to inform future research in this area.

constraints: The framework is scoped to the college classroom context

article_title: Self-regulated learning strategies predict learner behavior and goal attainment in Massive Open Online Courses
citation: Kizilcec, R. F., Pérez-Sanagustín, M., & Maldonado, J. J. (2017). Self-regulated learning strategies predict learner behavior and goal attainment in Massive Open Online Courses. Computers & Education, 104, 18–33. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.10.001
title: Pintrich's model of self-regulated learning as three categories of trainable strategies
description: The article adopts Pintrich's (2000) model, which defines SRL as "an active, constructive process whereby learners set goals for their learning and then attempt to monitor, regulate and control their cognition, intentions and behavior". The model identifies three categories of strategies learners apply to regulate learning: cognitive strategies (rehearsal, critical thinking, organization, elaboration), metacognitive strategies (goal setting and strategic planning, self-monitoring, self-evaluation), and resource management strategies (time management, help seeking, effort regulation). The authors chose this model over Zimmerman's phase model because its focus on particular strategies suits large-scale quantitative investigation that can inform targeted interventions.
requirements: SRL is treated as a trainable skill, not a fixed trait, developed through experience and practice applying SRL strategies
constraints: The model's strategy focus was chosen for quantitative tractability rather than as a claim about phase-based accounts being wrong
target_learners: adult online learners in self-paced MOOCs
target_learning_goals: attainment of personal course goals such as certification, assessment completion, and lecture completion
examples: The study operationalized six strategy subscales (goal setting, strategic planning, self-evaluation, task strategies, elaboration, help seeking) in a 23-item survey with Cronbach's alpha of at least 0.75

article_title: The Role of Goal Orientation in Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Paul R. Pintrich. (2000). The Role of Goal Orientation in Self-Regulated Learning. Handbook of Self-Regulation, Academic Press. https://www.elsevier.com
title: Pintrich's four-phase, four-area framework for self-regulated learning
description: The chapter proposes a general SRL framework displayed as a table crossing four phases of regulation with four areas for regulation. The phases are described as follows: "Phase 1 involves planning and goal setting as well as activation of perceptions and knowledge of the task and context and the self in relationship to the task," followed by monitoring, control and regulation, and reactions and reflections. The columns cover cognition, motivation/affect, behavior, and context, with the context column included because the personal self actively attempts to monitor and change the environment.
requirements: Learners must be assumed able to monitor, control, and regulate aspects of their own cognition, motivation, behavior, and environment
constraints: The phases are a heuristic; the chapter states there is no strong assumption that the phases are hierarchically or linearly structured such that earlier phases always must occur before later phases
target_learners: students in school and classroom contexts
target_learning_goals: academic learning across domains
self-regulation of cognition, motivation, behavior, and context

article_title: Reading, Writing, and Phonological Processing Skills of Adolescents With 10 or More Years of Cochlear Implant Experience
citation: Geers Ann E.; Hayes Heather. (2011). Reading, Writing, and Phonological Processing Skills of Adolescents with 10 or More Years of Cochlear Implant Experience. Ear and Hearing. https://doi.org/10.1097/AUD.0b013e3181fa41fa
title: Picture Spelling Test with phonological plausibility scoring
description: A researcher-designed spelling assessment created because traditional dictation spelling tasks are problematic for deaf children, since "it is difficult to know whether the word was accurately perceived". One hundred familiar, picturable words of varied orthographic length and complexity were presented as photographs, line drawings, or cartoons, and students spelled the named item. A companion phonological plausibility score quantified whether misspellings used plausible letters for each phoneme, referenced to an aligned corpus of word frequencies and pronunciations.
requirements: Items must be picturable and familiar to adolescent vocabulary
Scoring requires an aligned corpus of word frequencies matched with pronunciations to judge phoneme plausibility
constraints: Designed for and used with adolescents with prelingual deafness; accuracy scores cannot disentangle perception from spelling in dictation formats, which motivated the picture format
target_learners: adolescents with prelingual deafness and cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: spelling accuracy
phonological encoding of spoken words in writing
examples: Administered to 112 CI-HS students and 46 hearing controls; CI students spelled 67% of items correctly versus 80% for controls, and 62% of their errors were phonologically plausible versus 89% for controls

article_title: Tracking Grade 10 learners’ geometric reasoning through folding back
citation: Mabotja, S., Chuene, K., Maoto, S., & Kibirige, I. (2018). Tracking Grade 10 learners' geometric reasoning through folding back. Pythagoras, 39(1), a371. https://doi.org/10.4102/pythagoras.v39i1.371
title: Pirie and Kieren's dynamical theory of the growth of mathematical understanding
description: Pirie and Kieren's (1994) dynamical theory describes the growth of mathematical understanding through eight nested levels: primitive knowing, image making, image having, property noticing, formalising, observing, structuring and inventising. The article states that 'the growth in mathematical understanding is neither linear nor unidirectional' and that each layer contains the preceding layer and is contained in the layer that follows. The study used the first five levels to locate learners' understanding during geometry proof tasks, and folding back is the theory's mechanism for back-and-forth movement across layers.
requirements: Learners bring prior knowledge (primitive knowing) to their learning context, which serves as the innermost layer from which understanding grows.
constraints: The article notes Martin (2008) viewed Pirie and Kieren's definition of folding back as having 'remained essentially undeveloped and unelaborated in their work', so how and why folding back occurs is not deeply explored in the original theory.
target_learning_goals: Geometric reasoning and proof
Growth of mathematical understanding
examples: The article pitched the triangle-similarity proof task at the formalising level and interpreted learners' F-shape mnemonic use as working at the property noticing level.

article_title: Effects of two differently sequenced classroom scripts on common ground in collaborative inquiry learning
citation: Esther Tan (2018). Effects of two differently sequenced classroom scripts on common ground in collaborative inquiry learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9460-6
title: Two differently sequenced classroom scripts: PISG (Plenary–Individual–Small Group) and PSGI (Plenary–Small Group–Individual)
description: Both scripts begin with the teacher modeling each inquiry skill at the plenary level, then distribute activities across social levels in opposite orders. In this study, "students in the Plenary–Individual–Small Group (PISG) classroom script first worked individually before working in small groups, whereas students in the Plenary–Small Group–Individual (PSGI) condition first worked in small groups before working individually." Both sequences ran through a pre-field trip, field trip to the Botanical Gardens and post-field trip phase on plant adaptation, with inquiry task 1 consistently used for plenary teacher modeling. The scripts are used as macro-scripts that shape interaction patterns by sequencing tasks across plenary, individual and small group levels.
requirements: Each phase began with plenary teacher modeling of the targeted inquiry skills before the script transition; the script sequence was strictly adhered to from pre- to post-field trip.
constraints: In the PSGI condition, two groups experienced dropouts in the post-field trip; implementation spanned seven lessons of approximately 45 minutes over 2–3 weeks.
target_learners: students in grades 6–9 in a collaborative science inquiry unit
target_learning_goals: inquiry processes of generating and evaluating evidence and drawing conclusions, supported by grounding and testing
examples: PISG students first worked individually on inquiry task 2 (plants in the tropical rainforest) before small-group work on inquiry task 3 (plants in the desert); PSGI students did the reverse.

article_title: Pictures in Mathematical Word Problems: A Systematic Review on the Role of Task and Student Characteristics
citation: Terhi Vessonen, Heidi Hellstrand, Pirjo Aunio, Anu Laine. (2026). Pictures in Mathematical Word Problems: A Systematic Review on the Role of Task and Student Characteristics. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10112-5
title: Three-function taxonomy of provided pictures in word problems: representational, decorative, and informative
description: The review adopts a three-category taxonomy of provided pictures following Schewior and Lindner: "pictures are divided into three categories: representational, decorative, and informative". Representational pictures present the task situation or its mathematical structures (pictorial or schematic, static or dynamic); decorative pictures bear little to no relation to the specific task; informative pictures provide essential information additional to the text. The taxonomy organizes the review's coding and findings about when each picture type helps or harms performance.
requirements: Pictures must be provided rather than self-generated for this taxonomy to apply as coded in the review
constraints: Separating representational from organizational pictures is described as theoretically and practically challenging, so they are collapsed
target_learners: elementary school students in grades 1 to 6
target_learning_goals: mathematical word problem-solving skills
examples: The review coded each included study's pictures into these categories, additionally coding pictorial versus schematic and static versus dynamic dimensions

citation: Giang Pham, Franziska Maria Locher, Dimitra Kolovou, Eliane Arnold. (2026). COVID-19: A cross-national analysis with PISA data. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102366. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102366

constraints: Country-level ICCs were low (M = .06), and the article notes small differences between countries may attain statistical significance due to small standard errors
target_learning_goals: Measuring teaching and learning conditions for sustaining learning during COVID-19 school closures
examples: Items ST348–ST354 with response options from Never to Every day or almost every day, and Strongly disagree to Strongly agree

citation: Arens, A. Katrin; Morin, Alexandre J. S.; Watermann, Rainer. (2015). Relations between classroom disciplinary problems and student motivation. Achievement as a potential mediator? Learning and instruction 39. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.07.001

citation: Drew B. Headley and Denis Paré. (2017). Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple memory systems. npj Science of Learning 2:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0001-2
title: PING mechanism: gamma oscillations generated by pyramidal-interneuron reciprocal interaction
description: The review describes two candidate gamma generation mechanisms, interneuron-network gamma (ING) and pyramidal-ING (PING), regarding PING as the in vivo mechanism. requirements: Reciprocal connectivity between local pyramidal cells and inhibitory interneurons, with excitatory drive sufficient to recruit interneurons each cycle
constraints: ING alone is generally not considered to generate gamma in the intact brain; striatal gamma origin (intrinsic versus cortically imposed) remains unresolved

examples: The review notes optogenetically silencing PV basket cells reduces gamma evoked by principal cell activation

title: Developed pictured-letters training program with educational plans, worksheets, and three equivalent achievement tests
description: The authors developed a training program for teaching the 26 similar English letters under three methods: modified pictured letters, modified plus abstract letters, and traditional teaching. description: The article adopts the motivational scale of Pintrich et al. article_title: An Investigation into the Recognition and Production of Pitch Patterns of "If"-Clauses by Turkish Pre-Service Teachers of English
citation: Topal, İ.H. (2018). An investigation into the recognition and production of pitch patterns of if-clauses by turkish pre-service teachers of english. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(4), 285-300. http://www.jlls.org
title: Pitch-level and intonation-contour framework for English If-clauses (Discourse Intonation Model perspective)
description: The article presents a four-level pitch framework (Low /1/, Normal /2/, High /3/, Extra High /4/ pitch phonemes) in which levels combine into intonation contours. It states that "these pitch levels do not bear any meanings alone. Instead, they come together and form patterns through which phrases, clauses, and sentences are made." Within this framework, If-conditional sentences take the /2 3 2→/ - /2 3 1↓/ pattern when the If-clause precedes the main clause and two words carry primary stress, and the /2 3 1↓/ pattern when only one word is stressed. The instruction is contextualized in Brazil's Discourse Intonation Model, which connects intonation to discourse function.
requirements: Instruction must be contextualized in the light of the Discourse Intonation Model (Brazil, 1997), which deals with the communicative function of intonation
target_learners: Turkish pre-service teachers of English (freshman ELT students)
target_learning_goals: Recognizing and producing the pitch patterns of English If-clauses
examples: The study's 12-sentence corpus was annotated with /232→231/ or /231/ contours and illustrated with speech waves in Figures 1-12.

description: A time-pressured picture-cued writing test was used to measure learners' implicit knowledge of English articles. The Target-Like-Use formula (Pica, 1991) was applied to calculate accuracy of use. Three different sets of sequential pictures were used for pretest, Posttest 1, and Posttest 2 to investigate whether written CF helps learners improve their linguistic accuracy in a new piece of writing.

Time pressure of 30 minutes

examples: Three different sets of sequential pictures were used for pretest, Posttest 1, and Posttest 2 to avoid learners' negative reactions to writing the same story three times

description: The P-I-T-D-S model is a five-step extended flipped classroom framework for dental preclinical education built around a virtual simulation system. target_learning_goals: Recognizing primary immunodeficiency disease, linking immune system dysfunction to clinical manifestations, and initial patient management

title: Pig transport institutional-framework role play for engineering ethics
description: A two-round role play based on the 2007 Dutch political controversy around irregularities in cattle transport and the inspection-versus-self-regulation debate concerning the Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (VWA). target_learning_goals: recognizing moral problems in professional practice
awareness of different dimensions in decision making
thinking about institutional frameworks for responsible action
examples: In a second version, the authors simplified the institutional alternatives by offering students different scenarios to specify and elaborate, and several concrete proposals came to the fore and were discussed.
